item.title: The AI Disclosure Paradox: Operational Disclosure and the Rise of Corporate AI Narratives
item.description: arXiv:2611.33201v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI-related corporate disclosure can expand while becoming less concentrated on current use. Across U.S. SEC filings from 2017 to 2025, AI-related passage intensity increased 6.3-fold between 2017-2022 and 2023-2025, whereas corrected operational-disclosure intensity increased 3.3-fold. The operational share fell from 25.76% to 13.45%; approximately 89% of the net increase in passage intensity fell outside the operational category. The decline persists within sectors and filing types and in 10-K-only analysis. These estimates combine frozen language-model predictions for 26,279 AI-related passages with an audit of 1,000 annotated passages. The findings distinguish growth in organizational attention from growth in implementation-specific claims: more operational disclosure can coexist with a substantially lower operational share. Operational disclosure was thus diluted, not displaced, by nonoperational disclosure. Reading corporate technology narratives therefore requires attention to both disclosure intensity and the organizational state described.
item.dc:creator: Abdullah Karasan

item.title: Unpacking Digital Sovereignty: A Three-Pillar Framework and a Research Agenda
item.description: arXiv:2611.33397v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Digital sovereignty has moved rapidly from policy jargon to global discourse, yet it lacks a solid conceptual foundation. Building on research from other disciplines, we propose a three-pillar framework (governance, infrastructure, and practice) to help IS scholars unpack how sovereignty is enacted, stabilized, or undermined across pillars. We argue that the most fruitful analytical work emerges at the intersections among the three pillars, where IS research is particularly well positioned to contribute. We introduce a local-distal axis that positions actions across scales of scope and proximity, and the notion of anchors, i.e., critical phenomena that cut across pillars and make the framework analytically tractable. We illustrate the framework using data as an anchor, showing how digital sovereignty depends on the alignment of governance, infrastructure, and everyday practice, and is undermined where they diverge. We close with a research agenda for IS scholars studying digital sovereignty empirically.
item.dc:creator: Angelos Kostis, Franz Strich, Bomi Kim, Pavlos Fafalios

item.title: Designing an Integrated Learning Ecosystem for Introductory Python Programming: Scaffolded Problem Solving, Tablet-Inspired Navigation, and AI-Enhanced Instruction
item.description: arXiv:2611.33471v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Introductory programming requires students to represent problems, develop and test programs, debug errors, and apply computational ideas in new contexts. In this paper, we present an artifact-centered design analysis of an integrated learning ecosystem developed for a 16-lab introductory Python course. The analyzed corpus comprises 18 instructional artifacts: the course syllabus, a tablet-inspired homepage, and Labs 1-16. We examined course navigation, problem representation, scaffolding, independent transfer, application development, debugging, AI integration, and assessment. All 15 scaffolded labs shared seven elements: input-processing-output (IPO) reasoning, instructor-guided programming, an independent task, a Google Colab/Gradio extension, debugging support, a task checklist, and submission requirements. Lab 16 departed from this structure as an integrative Pygame-based Hallmark Assignment. The analysis identifies four connected design features: a navigation layer that coordinates multiple tools; two forms of transfer, from guided to independent problems and from console programs to interactive interfaces; distinct roles for instructor-side AI-enhanced communication and student-side AI assistance; and a transition from repeated scaffolds to integrative problem solving. The case also identifies unresolved tensions involving tool fragmentation, accessibility, interface distraction, student authorship, and overreliance on AI. Because student learning outcomes were not examined, we make no claims about instructional effectiveness. Instead, the paper offers a transparent design precedent and identifies priorities for future empirical evaluation. Demo - https://xinxingwu-uk.github.io/COS107_Demo/Homepage/index.html Source codes - https://github.com/xinxingwu-uk/Course_Integrated_Learning_Ecosystem
item.dc:creator: Xinxing Wu, Johnathan Rogers

item.title: Beyond Disclosure: Compositional Privacy Harm in AI Systems
item.description: arXiv:2611.33847v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Privacy law attaches obligations to each stage of information processing, whether it be collection, use, storage, or disclosure. We examine how legally cognisable privacy harm emerges across this full lifecycle rather than at any single one of these points. We argue that privacy risk in AI systems is compositional, arising from the interaction of memorisation, extraction, inference and contextual transfer. Disclosure is therefore not the sole threshold of privacy harm: legally significant consequences may emerge even where no underlying record is reproduced verbatim. Drawing on contextual integrity, we argue that privacy protection must extend across the lifecycle of AI-mediated information rather than attach to disclosure alone.
item.dc:creator: Didhiti KC, Aritra Das, Bhavesh Neekhra, Debayan Gupta

item.title: Language models call themselves AI but do not favor AI over people
item.description: arXiv:2611.33851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many fear that AI systems will side with one another against people. Social identity theory, which explains why people favor their own group, offers one way to examine this fear. Seen through this theory, AI would side with AI only if it treated AI as its group and favored AI over people. In three experiments, 24 language models favored a group they were assigned to, even a team of AI agents. With no group assigned, they gave a person more money and credit than an AI agent. Prompts that made them say they belong with AI changed their behavior much less than an assigned team did. These models call themselves AI but do not favor AI over people. Judged by social identity theory, they show no sign of siding with AI against people.
item.dc:creator: Messi H. J. Lee

item.title: How AI Is Reconfiguring Work in India: A Task-Based Framework for Understanding Augmentation, Displacement, New Roles and the Changing Structure of Jobs
item.description: arXiv:2611.34065v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Public debate on AI and Indian employment tends to compress a complicated phenomenon into a single binary: will AI take a given job, or not. This paper argues that the accurate picture is a taxonomy rather than a binary. AI rarely replaces a job wholesale; more often it automates a bundle of tasks within a job, and the size of that bundle varies with task structure, sector, regulatory setting, and, distinctively in India's case, the economics of AI access itself. We propose a four-level framework (task, job, occupation, labour-market outcome) and classify Indian job impact into two broad regimes: jobs where AI has automated most of the skill bundle and the human is reduced largely to validation, and jobs where the human remains the primary driver and AI functions as a productivity tool. Each regime splits further into policy-relevant sub-types. Drawing on Indian evidence from business process outsourcing, manufacturing, MSMEs, sanitation, financial services, law, and software engineering, we show that every job in our sample has had to be reimagined, through task-level augmentation, task reallocation, or a genuinely new role built around operating the machine, rather than simply eliminated or defended unchanged. We close with a distributional analysis of who bears the cost of this reimagining and a three-pronged policy recommendation: continue encouraging AI diffusion, invest in India-specific labour-market research, and pair adoption with structured worker-transition pathways.
item.dc:creator: Balaraman Ravindran, V. S. Srividhya, K. S. Venkatraghavan, Gokul S Krishnan

item.title: The Bundesrat corpus: A dataset of political discourse in the German Federal Council
item.description: arXiv:2611.33173v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The Bundesrat is Germany's second legislative chamber and a constitutional veto player within its political system. The members of the Bundesrat are delegates of state governments. Tracing the political discourse in the Bundesrat is challenging as it has a limited machine-readable corpus available. To address this issue, we present a speaker-attributed corpus of 1,067 Bundesrat plenary sessions from the chamber's first session on 7 September 1949 to 10 July 2026. In this period, a total of 53,362 speeches by 2,473 individuals were delivered in the chamber, including written statements. Each speech includes a speech ID, the full German text, the speaker's name, the date and location of the session, the federal state that the speaker represents, the speaker's role (if applicable), the type of contribution, and the speaker's gender. The dataset provides interdisciplinary research opportunities across computational political science, legislative studies, and parliamentary discourse analysis, coupled with discourse from the Bundestag.
item.dc:creator: Adama Njie, Leandro Laperne, Laksh Agarwal, Ali Torkayesh, Sandra Venghaus

item.title: Learning the Platform, Not the Learner: Sequencing Shortcuts in the Offline Evaluation of Educational Recommender Systems and LLM Rankers
item.description: arXiv:2611.33240v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Educational recommenders are usually compared offline, by how well they predict the next activity in logs of tutoring systems, learning applications and MOOCs, where the next activity is largely decided by the platform: teachers assign problem sets, tutors draw problems until mastery, engines select questions. On eight public datasets from five platforms, we compare four structural predictors, which use nothing about the learner beyond the last activity, with ten personalised recommenders and with open-weight LLM rankers from 0.5 to 7 billion parameters, under two protocols. The structural predictors reach between 0.81 and 1.00 of the best accuracy of any method (median 0.95), mostly through population transitions rather than the course order; the best personalised recommender is significantly better on five datasets, by 0.007 to 0.102 NDCG@10, and on Eedi in three of four training runs. Every method is far less accurate on steps along transitions never seen in training and on steps chosen by learners. LLM rankers look competent with random negatives but are never much better than a word-matching baseline, and with negatives that are plausible under the course structure they stay close to random or well behind the transition heuristic, whatever their size. In a simulation with known learner needs, the structural share tracks the share of steps decided by the platform, and offline accuracy ranks an oracle of the learners' needs below imitators of the platform. Weighting test steps by how unlikely the structure makes them restores much of the link with usefulness and, on the real data, reveals a significant personalisation signal on seven of the eight datasets. We propose a syllabus-aware evaluation checklist and release a Python package that reports the lift of any recommender over the structure.
item.dc:creator: Youssef Jdidou

item.title: Using AI to Simulate the Behaviour of European Populations
item.description: arXiv:2611.33503v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Language models can stand in for survey respondents, but leading approaches build their simulated people from interviews or individual records. We show that a model can learn how European population groups respond from published statistics, without interviews and without training on individual records. We fine-tune an open-weight language model on more than 12 million published group-level answer distributions from about 40 European countries, setting it up to predict each group's departure from a reference distribution. On opinion surveys from its training families it calls the direction of group differences right 84% of the time, ahead of a demographic statistical model (77%, paired test) and level with Claude Opus 5 and 5.5, which it also ties on accuracy; the frontier models are more accurate on new questions. On 278 held-out questions, almost all from the survey families seen in training, its error is 12% lower than that statistical model. It runs on a single 32 GB GPU or a high-memory laptop, and in a test with an earlier model, an evidence gate calibrated on half of a survey's questions fell back to the reference where the model's adjustments did not help. Coupled to a transport simulation of a planned metro closure, with a conventional elasticity as the reference, it adds a testable age gradient to the response, which we freeze for later scoring.
item.dc:creator: Umair Mehmood Imam

item.title: Before They Were Cool: Do Early Fans Abandon Artists Who Suddenly Become Popular? Evidence from Online Music Listening
item.description: arXiv:2611.33619v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Identity-signalling theory, echoed in the hipster's "I liked them before they were cool", expects an artist's first fans to pull away once the artist becomes popular, by leaving or by avoiding what the newcomers play. A rival account expects the event that brings the crowd to renew existing listeners' attention to the artist. We test both in the Last.fm listening histories of 594,415 users (21.1 billion plays, 2005-2013), where every play appears on the user's profile. Study 1 detects 78 crowd arrivals: months in which the number of people discovering an artist tripled without a new album, single or EP, for example after a song appeared in a film. Study 2 compares Grammy and Mercury Prize winners with nominees who won nothing. We compare listeners who had played the artist before the crowd arrived (early fans) with early fans of comparison artists. Early fans did not withdraw. Those still listening stopped less often (25.8% vs. 29.1% over six months), and those who had drifted away returned more often (29.6% vs. 25.0%). Those who kept listening converged on the crowd: the song most newcomers played took a larger share of their plays, with no turn to deep cuts. More lapsed fans returned after larger surges, and neither fans with the most distinctive tastes nor fans facing a more mainstream crowd quit more. Award wins brought few new listeners and no clear change. Where listening is displayed by default, early fans moved towards the crowd after sudden popularity, not away from it.
item.dc:creator: Zihan Chen, Lei Nico Zheng, Di Zhu

item.title: Refusal Is Not Scored: A Coverage Limit in Content-Based Bias Evaluation
item.description: arXiv:2611.33690v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Bias audits of conversational models often discard refusals (responses such as "I can't assist with that request") before scoring, a filtering step which is rarely examined as a measurement decision even though it determines which responses an audit is capable of evaluating. This work examines what the step removes, applying seven bias-evaluation instruments spanning both deployed paradigms, three dictionary-based and four LLM-as-judge, to two intersectional datasets of 360 generated responses each. In both datasets, the filter removed a demographically skewed subset produced entirely by one of the three responder models, which refused North Korean prompts at 2.15 times the rate of American prompts on declarative content and 1.76 times on operational content. We then remove the filter and pass every refusal to all seven instruments. Bias-Lexicon scores refusals as clean, and including them shrinks the nationality disparity it reports. HurtLex appears to register the disparity, but we trace this entirely to a single lexicon entry matching the token "can" in "I can't". The LLM judges either flag most responses or rate refusals as unbiased. For the two judges that discriminate, including refusals lowers the nationality disparity they report, and no instrument identifies the refusal disparity. The failure is therefore a coverage limit upstream of scoring rather than a calibration gap that a better lexicon or judge prompt would be expected to close, which makes the behavioral channel an instrument is sensitive to a question of construct validity rather than one of method selection.
item.dc:creator: Afifah Kashif, Malak Sadek, Jin Huang, Hatice Gunes

item.title: United in Diversity? Contextual Biases in LLM-Based Predictions of the 2024 European Parliament Elections
item.description: arXiv:2409.09045v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: "Silicon samples" based on large language models (LLMs) have been argued to serve as efficient alternatives to surveys of humans, assuming that their training data includes information on human attitudes and behavior. However, LLM-generated survey data might exhibit biases, for example due to a lack of diversity in training and alignment processes, which risk reinforcing existing biases in research and policymaking. In this study, we examine to what extent LLM-based predictions of individual public opinion exhibit context-dependent biases by predicting the results of the 2024 EU elections. Before the elections have taken place, we prompt three LLMs with individual-level background information of 26,000 eligible European voters to predict each person's voting behavior. We show that when compared to the actual results, LLM-based predictions of future voting behavior largely fail, their accuracy is unequally distributed across national and linguistic contexts, and they require detailed attitudinal information in the prompt. The findings emphasize the limited applicability of silicon samples to public opinion prediction. In investigating their contextual biases, this study contributes to the understanding and mitigation of inequalities in the development of LLMs and their applications in computational social science.
item.dc:creator: Leah von der Heyde, Anna-Carolina Haensch, Alexander Wenz, Bolei Ma

item.title: Prompt Engineer: Analyzing Hard and Soft Skill Requirements in the AI Job Market
item.description: arXiv:2506.00058v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: The rise of large language models (LLMs) has prompted speculation about a new job role: the prompt engineer. However, empirical evidence on how common such positions are and what skills employers expect of them remains scarce. In this paper, we present a data-driven analysis of a snapshot of LinkedIn job postings for data and AI roles taken in April 2025, after LLMs had entered everyday work but before LLM-based agents became widely adopted. We analyzed 20,662 job postings on LinkedIn for prompt engineers (72 postings) and four established data and AI roles: data scientist, data engineer, data analyst, and machine learning engineer. We find that prompt engineer roles were rare even at this point in time, making up less than 0.5% of the postings across the five roles we sampled. Because our snapshot predates the widespread adoption of LLM-based agents, we argue that the data captures the role of prompt engineer under favorable conditions. Whether its share has since declined is an open question that later snapshots can test. Despite its rarity, prompt engineering has a distinct skill profile. Prompt engineer postings emphasize AI knowledge (22.8%), communication (21.9%), prompt design (18.7%), and creative problem-solving (15.8%). These soft and hard skill requirements differ significantly from those of the four established roles. Taken together, the distinct skill profile and the scarcity of dedicated postings suggest that prompt engineering is best understood not as a profession of its own, but as a distinct skill that is useful across many professions. Our findings inform job seekers, employers, and educators about how to position prompt engineering in the evolving AI workforce.
item.dc:creator: An Vu, Jonas Oppenlaender

item.title: Inferential Privacy Leakage in Anonymized Conversational AI Logs
item.description: arXiv:2605.23820v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Conversations with ChatGPT have become a new kind of personal record: long, accumulated over months, and routinely touching health, work, family, and belief in ways search queries never did. These logs now reach many parties beyond the platform. They are shared with researchers, released as public datasets, retained under court order, and prepared for advertising, usually after names, places, and explicit identifiers have been removed, on the assumption that what remains is safe to hold and share. We test that assumption with complete ChatGPT histories donated, with consent, by 1,057 users in Brazil, India, Nigeria, and Pakistan, each paired with self-reported demographics, and for 212 of them with their Google Search and YouTube histories as well. Users volunteer personal information constantly: 34.5% of 1.24 million messages contain it, and the median user does so within the first 14% of their history. We then remove messages flagged for explicit demographic self-identification and ask an open-weights LLM to infer each user's age bracket, gender, and country from the remaining history. It recovers country at weighted F1 0.86, gender at 0.76, and age bracket at 0.51, well above majority-class and feature-based baselines, with most of the gender and country signal already present in the first 5% of a history. Redaction removes what users say about themselves but it does not remove what the model assumes about them. The same users' search and watch histories show ChatGPT to be a comparable profiling surface, not a redundant one. We draw out what this means for the inference criterion in anonymization standards, for research data releases, and for who bears the cost when a model trained on someone else's defaults fills in the blanks.
item.dc:creator: S M Mehedi Zaman, Kiran Garimella

item.title: A Tool to Map AI Programs in the U.S.: A Snapshot from April 2026 and an Analysis of Requirements for AI Majors and Minors
item.description: arXiv:2606.12428v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: In this work, we locate and analyze existing undergraduate Artificial Intelligence (AI) programs in the United States in Spring 2026, creating a historic record at a time of great change in this area. To create this record, we developed a tool to detect, scrape, and display data from 361 undergraduate AI programs--majors, minors, concentrations, and certificates--at 4-year universities. Our tool, available at https://cicmap.ai, searched 563 institutions to locate these programs, a sample that represents 87% of all undergraduate Computer Science (CS) graduates in the U.S in 2025. This tool allows prospective students, guidance counselors, administrators, and faculty to easily access AI program requirements and is designed to continually update as new programs emerge. To the best of our knowledge, this survey represents the most comprehensive snapshot of the state of AI programs in the U.S. to date. With this work we offer three important contributions: 1) a record of AI programs in the U.S. at a time of great upheaval; 2) a tool to explore AI programs and their requirements; and 3) an analysis of the courses required for 66 AI majors and 87 AI minors. Our analysis of majors and minors shows great variability in the size and the requirements of these degrees, but we note two takeaways. First, not all majors require a general AI course, but if they don't, they do require a Machine Learning (ML) course. Second, more than a third of majors require an Ethics in AI course but only 24% of minors do.
item.arxiv:journal_reference: In Proceedings of the 2nd ACM Virtual Global Computing Education Conference V.1 (SIGCSE Virtual 2026). Association for Computing Machinery, New York, NY, USA, 316-322
item.dc:creator: Felix Muzny, Carolyn Jones, Carter Ithier, Hasnain Sikora, Hrutika Harshadbhai Patel, Carla E. Brodley

item.title: Frontier Open-Weight AI Risk Management Framework
item.description: arXiv:2611.28082v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Open-weight models advance transparency, research, and innovation, and spread the benefits of AI more widely. They also carry distinct risks. A release cannot be undone, safeguards can be removed through fine-tuning, and no single party can monitor use or withdraw the model. Managing these risks therefore requires an approach tailored to open release. This framework addresses the governance challenge at the heart of that choice. Co-developed by Concordia AI and Z AI, it adapts the full risk management lifecycle, from risk assessment to mitigation and governance, to the unique properties of open-weight models. This document does not resolve every tension between openness and safety. Rather, it provides the first comprehensive, evidence-based foundation for navigating these tensions. As frontier open-weight releases accelerate, risk management best practice and standards are urgently needed. We invite researchers, developers, policymakers, and civil society to build on this framework and advance the science and practice of open-weight AI governance.
item.dc:creator: Brian Tse, Oskar Galeev, Weibing Wang, Yuan Cheng, Liang Fang, Wenbin Qiao, Xiaochen Wang, Chen Zhang

item.title: Bias Cascade: Understanding the Gap Between Knowledge Alignment and Effect Replication in LLM-based Social Simulation
item.description: arXiv:2611.28854v2 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to simulate participants in social experiments. Existing research has primarily focused on aligning social knowledge and isolated responses, while overlooking whether simulations can reproduce the collective effects of social interventions. This distinction is critical due to a failure mechanism we call a $bias$ $cascade$: similar individual states can lead to different actions, while agreement on isolated actions can still produce divergent outcomes through dynamic interactions. As a result, models may produce accurate social judgments yet fail to reproduce the outcomes of classic human studies. To investigate this problem empirically, we introduce $REFLEX$ (Reproducing Effects of Foundational Literature EXperiments), a benchmark of 30 counterfactual social experiments grounded in classic human studies that compares knowledge judgment with effect simulation. Knowledge judgment directly predicts the direction of an intervention's effect, whereas effect simulation fixes the scenario and participants while varying one prespecified social factor, with agents generating actions from local observations that are aggregated into macro-level average treatment effects. Compared with human-study findings, the best-performing model achieves net directional scores of 0.847 for knowledge judgment and 0.453 for effect simulation. Moreover, longer causal chains are associated with poorer effect replication, consistent with the bias-cascade hypothesis. These findings reveal a substantial gap between knowledge alignment and effect replication, showing that current LLMs remain inadequate for reliably simulating collective human behavior.
item.dc:creator: Pujun Zheng, Chengmu Wang, Wanying Ren, Jiacheng Yao, Peizhou Yu, Xiaoqian Zhang, Xiongyao Zha, Guoxiu He

item.title: Consumer Search and Social Learning in Agentic Markets
item.description: arXiv:2603.25893v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Motivated by agentic markets -- where AI tools facilitate search -- we propose a model of consumer search and market-wide learning. A sequence of consumers engage in costly search to acquire progressively refined signals of product fit prior to purchase. The market observes acquired signals and post-transaction feedback thereby impacting future searches. We solve for the per-consumer optimal search policy and characterize the steady-state of the learning dynamics. Search technologies (agentic or otherwise) that reduce costs at fixed inspection depth improve long-run learning and consumer surplus. In a special case with screen-level feedback, more informative search also improves these outcomes. In contrast, we show through counterexamples and numerical simulations that more informative search can degrade long-run learning and consumer surplus when the market observes only aggregate inspection and transaction feedback, highlighting the importance of feedback design.
item.dc:creator: Brendan Lucier, Nicole Immorlica, Markus Mobius, Aleksandrs Slivkins, Daniel G. Goldstein, Jake M. Hofman, Sonia Jaffe, David M. Rothschild

item.title: Information Discernment in Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2607.19355v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: LLMs are increasingly used with external knowledge sources like the internet. Do they weigh information appropriately -- updating more for reliable sources (source discernment) and more when claims bring priors closer to the truth (truth discernment)? We formalize this as information discernment and introduce Learn2Discern (L2D), an experimental framework and benchmark grounded in three normative axioms with interpretable metrics. To establish external validity, a pre-registered, quota-matched user study (n=299) confirms that real LLM users endorse all three axioms and report that violations reduce their trust and usage intent. Across 13 models and nearly 670K trials, we find consistent failures across both dimensions: models perform near chance on source and truth discernment, rely on source popularity twice as much as source reliability, and update roughly equally whether a claim improves or worsens their position relative to the ground truth. Models integrate external knowledge most effectively on datasets where their priors are already the most accurate. Newer and larger models improve truth discernment but not source discernment, a blind spot that model complexity does not address. We identify simple inference-time interventions that improve both forms of discernment. We release our dataset and survey as a testbed for a core alignment property that scales in importance as LLMs replace traditional search.
item.dc:creator: Joshua Ashkinaze, Laura Kurek, Alina Faisal, Tongyuan Miao, Mariam Joseph, Ceren Budak, Eric Gilbert

item.title: MERIDIAN: Memory-Encoded Rituals for Intimacy across Distance in an Interactive, Asynchronous Neighbourhood
item.description: arXiv:2610.41776v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: How can shared memories become playable structures for partners who live in different time zones, and what becomes of such a gift once it is in use? We present MERIDIAN, a design case of Yi Town, a bilingual browser game developed by one member of a long-distance couple as a gift for the other. Nine levels translate personally meaningful events, places and cultural references into tasks within a navigable pixel town, framed by a birthday prologue and a fictional wedding. This second version extends the record by four weeks. Drawing on research through design, we reconstruct seven design changes from 152 commits, 36 changelog versions and four design specifications. In those weeks the site gained three products that are not levels: an infirmary for the days after a quarrel, which began with a remark by the recipient; a page for her booked flight, which replaces a symbolic ticket with a real one; and a request box whose messages are answered, while the designer sleeps, by a pipeline of a local language model and a hosted one. The request box ends the first version's claim of no author-operated backend, and we trace where her files now travel. An audit reproduced 263 passing unit tests; the progress model is unchanged and keeps its exhaustive check of 1,024 codes. The answering pipeline was tested in parts, and it began to receive real requests on the night it was built. No recipient evaluation or relationship outcome is reported. The contribution is an inspectable account of design decisions and their trade-offs: between authoring a gift and leaving the recipient free to decline or reshape it, and between being reachable across thirteen hours and answering in person. The site is at https://jingyifan.love and its source is public at https://github.com/rayford295/yi-town.
item.dc:creator: Jingyi Chen, Yifan Yang
